title: API Usage Meter
followUps: What is the time and space complexity of each operation? What is the worst case for memory, and how would you bound it?
Your meter keeps every request in the window. How would you approximate it with constant memory per key (fixed windows, sliding-window counters, or a token bucket), and what accuracy do you give up?
The API runs on 50 servers behind a load balancer. How would you enforce one quota per key across all of them, and what happens when the shared store is slow or down?
Product wants monthly billing based on these units. Why shouldn't the rate-limiting meter also be the billing record, and what would you build instead?
How would you return useful rate-limit information to developers (headers, error bodies, retry hints) so their clients back off correctly?

interviewer.approach: Hash map from API key to a FIFO queue of (timestamp, units) plus a running total per key. On each call for a key, pop from the front while the oldest entry's timestamp <= timestamp - windowSeconds, subtracting its units. consume compares total + units with quota; on success append and add. usage just expires and returns the total. Because timestamps never decrease, each event is pushed and popped at most once: amortized O(1) per call, O(events in window) space. Merging events with the same timestamp into one queue entry bounds memory at O(windowSeconds) per key. A circular buffer of per-second buckets is an equally good answer. Strong candidates mention approximate variants (sliding-window counter, token bucket) and the distributed version (Redis Lua script or INCR with expiry) unprompted.
hints: For one key, what do you need to remember to answer 'how many units in the last W seconds'?
Timestamps never go backwards. When an old request leaves the window, can it ever come back in?
Keep a queue of requests and a running total per key; drop expired requests from the front before you answer.
pitfalls: Recording a rejected request, so a client that's over quota stays blocked forever.
Off-by-one at the window edge: counting a request from exactly windowSeconds ago, or dropping one from windowSeconds - 1 ago.
Summing the whole history (or the whole queue) on every call: O(n) per call.
A single global queue for all keys, which makes expiry and totals tangled and slow.
Using the quota from the first call for the key instead of the one passed on each call.
Comparing usage + units < quota instead of <=, which rejects a request that exactly reaches the quota.

dimensions.name: Verifying the AI's window and quota semantics
dimensions.signals: Checked that the AI's code expires requests at exactly timestamp - windowSeconds (the old end is exclusive), does not record rejected requests, allows usage that exactly reaches the quota, and uses the per-call quota. Confirmed amortized O(1) rather than re-summing history, and could explain why the non-decreasing timestamps make the queue work.

levels.1: Accepted AI code with an off-by-one window or that records rejected requests.
levels.2: Found window or quota bugs only through failing hidden tests.
levels.3: Wrote boundary sequences (request at t, query at t + W - 1 and t + W) and a rejected-then-retry sequence before trusting the AI.
levels.4: Pinned down the window definition with the AI first, reviewed the expiry loop precisely, and discussed approximate and distributed variants.

watchFor: Expiry with < instead of <= (or vice versa), so a request exactly windowSeconds old is still counted.
Recording the request before checking the quota, or not rolling it back when rejected.
Re-summing a list of all requests on every call instead of keeping a running total.
Caching the quota per key from the first call.
Python answers that use list.pop(0) instead of a deque: O(n) per expiry.
